newsitem.title: SWEDEN: ABB sees economic trends dip in 2001.
newsitem.headline: ABB sees economic trends dip in 2001.

text.p: International engineering company ABB said on Friday it expected economic trends to pick up in 1998 only to fall around 2001.

"We will probably remain at these levels and then we think that we can see relatively good growth in 1998, 1999 and 2000," ABB chief executive Goran Lindahl told an analysts meeting, adding he expected a fall in 2001.

ABB reported a two percent rise in six-month net profit to $567 million which was below a market forecast of 4.5 percent. In local currencies, the rise was 12 percent and Lindahl said net effect on currencies was largely at that level.

Amongst individual businesses, power generation order intake and operating profit was expected to reach at least its 1996 level, while power transmission was seen improving order intake and operating profit, Lindahl said.
Industrial and building systems order intake was expected to level off this year while the operating profit was seen at unchanged levels.
ABB's international railway systems unit Adtranz was seen posting a stronger operating profit and order intake in 1997.
ABB is focusing more and more on service and modernisation, which now corresponds to 22 percent of total sales, Lindahl said.
"In the years 2000-2001 we will have doubled our share from $6 billion to $12 billion," he said adding that the company was still too dependent on the markets in Western Europe and North America.
"That part will be less than half as big in two to three years," Lindahl said.

ABB's order intake rose 14 percent to $20 billion in the first six months of the year. In the Middle East and Africa, order intake rose 50 percent to $2 billion. In Asia the upturn was 80 percent to $5.2 billion while Central and Eastern Europe rose 20 percent to $0.8 billion.
In Western Europe, order intake fell by seven percent to $8.8 billion and in North America it dropped three percent to $2.4 billion. South American order intake fell seven percent to $0.8 billion.
"Latin America was a bit of a disappointment. We should have had a growth of five or seven percent," Lindahl said.
"We must succeed in taking large (market) shares in this part of the world to grow," he said, adding that the growth potential was large in Latin America.
Industrial and building systems showed a market upturn across the entire product line, both in Latin America and Asia but Lindahl stressed that ABB's market shares were small.
"We can grow dramatically in Asia and Latin America without the market growing so I expect that we can continue growing even if the market levels off," Lindahl said.
